column2: **A memory-efficient cache system stores a complete binary tree with 1 million nodes in an array. Parent at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2. Node at index 500,000 is accessed. How many array positions away is its parent?**
column3: For node at index i, parent is at (i-1)//2. Node at 500,000 has parent at (500,000-1)//2 = 249,999. Distance = 500,000 - 249,999 = 250,001 positions. Array representation enables O(1) parent/child access through arithmetic. Trade-off: requires contiguous memory and works efficiently only for complete trees. Sparse trees waste significant space.
column14: 250,001 positions

column2: **A user authentication system stores 100K usernames in a BST. Marketing claims O(log n) guaranteed search time. Security audit finds worst-case login time correlates with insertion order. What causes this discrepancy?**
column3: BST search is O(h) where h=height. For balanced tree, h=log n giving O(log n). However, inserting sorted usernames creates skewed tree with h=n, degrading to O(n). Standard BST doesn't self-balance. Solution: use AVL or Red-Black tree guaranteeing O(log n) worst case through rotations. This is critical for systems where adversary controls insertion order.
column13: O(log n) guaranteed for all BSTs
column14: BST degenerates to O(n) with sorted insertions; needs self-balancing

column2: **An embedded system with 512KB RAM must traverse binary tree with 100K nodes in-order without recursion stack or auxiliary data structures. Morris traversal uses threaded tree technique. What is the space complexity?**
column3: Morris traversal temporarily modifies tree by creating threads (rightmost node of left subtree points to current node), traverses, then restores structure. Space O(1) as no stack/queue needed. Time O(n) but with larger constant due to thread creation/removal. Trade-off: O(1) space for tree modification overhead. Recursion uses O(h) stack; explicit stack uses O(h); Morris uses O(1).
column14: O(h) same as recursion

column2: **Two binary trees produce same preorder traversal: [1,2,3]. First tree: 1 has left child 2, which has left child 3 (left-skewed). Second tree: 1 has left child 2, which has right child 3. Level-order traversals differ. Why does preorder fail to uniquely identify structure?**
column3: Preorder visits root before children but doesn't encode NULL children. Both trees show 1→2→3 in preorder. Level-order shows [1,2,3] for first and [1,2,3] for second - also identical! Need both preorder AND inorder, or preorder with NULL markers to uniquely reconstruct. Single traversal insufficient as multiple structures can produce same sequence.
column14: Level-order is also ambiguous; need multiple traversals or NULL markers

column2: **A social network analyzes maximum separation between any two users in organization tree (diameter = longest path between any two nodes). Naive approach: for each node, find max depth left + max depth right, taking O(n²). What optimization reduces to O(n)?**
column3: Calculate diameter during single tree traversal. At each node, compute left_depth and right_depth recursively, updating global diameter = max(diameter, left_depth + right_depth + 2). Height calculation and diameter update combined in single pass. Avoids recalculating depths for every node. Time O(n), space O(h) for recursion.

column1: BST vs Hash Table Range Query
column2: **A stock trading system must support: (1) exact price lookup, (2) find all stocks in price range $50-$100. BST gives O(log n) exact lookup, O(log n + k) range query where k=results. Hash table gives O(1) lookup but O(n) range scan. With 1M stocks, which is better?**
column3: BST maintains sorted order enabling efficient range queries: find start with O(log n) search, then in-order traversal yields k results in O(k). Total O(log n + k). Hash table must scan all n entries checking each price - O(n) regardless of k. For range-heavy workloads, BST superior despite slower exact lookups. Many systems use both: hash for exact match, tree for ranges.
column13: Hash table always better with O(1)
column14: BST better for range queries O(log n + k) vs O(n) hash scan
column16: Depends on number of results only

column2: **Finding LCA of nodes P and Q in binary tree. Approach 1: Store path from root to P, path to Q, find last common node - O(n) time, O(h) space. Approach 2: Recursive check if P and Q in different subtrees - O(n) time, O(h) space. For BST, can we improve?**
column3: In BST, LCA search exploits ordering: if both P and Q < current, LCA in left subtree; if both > current, LCA in right; else current is LCA. Single path from root O(h), no path storage needed. For balanced BST, O(log n) time O(1) space. Regular binary tree requires O(n) as no ordering helps pruning search space.
column14: BST ordering enables O(h) time O(1) space traversal
column15: Both tree types require O(n) time
column16: LCA is always root in BST

column2: **A distributed cache serializes binary trees for network transmission. Preorder traversal with NULL markers: serialize([1,2,None,None,3]) = '1,2,#,#,3,#,#'. Is this sufficient for unique reconstruction?**
column3: Preorder with NULL markers encodes complete structure. Each NULL explicitly marks missing children, eliminating ambiguity. Deserialize rebuilds tree recursively consuming tokens. Single traversal with NULLs sufficient. Without NULLs, need two traversals (e.g., preorder + inorder). Trade-off: NULL markers increase serialized size but enable single-traversal reconstruction.
column14: Preorder with NULLs sufficient for unique reconstruction

column2: **A file system navigator needs frequent in-order successor queries for next file. Standard BST: finding in-order successor requires O(h) parent traversal. Threaded BST: right pointer of node without right child points to in-order successor. What's the trade-off?**
column3: Threaded BST enables O(1) in-order successor access via thread pointers. Space overhead: no additional space (reuses NULL right pointers). Cost: insertion/deletion complexity increases as threads must be maintained. Used when traversal frequency >> modification frequency. File browsers, iterators benefit from O(1) successor.
column13: No practical benefit over standard BST
column14: O(1) successor but complex insert/delete; useful when reads >> writes
column15: Requires O(n) extra space for threads

column2: **A heap implementation requires complete binary tree property. Developer creates tree where all levels filled except last, but last level has gaps (not left-filled). Heap operations fail. What property is violated?**
column3: Complete binary tree requires all levels filled except possibly last, AND last level filled left-to-right with no gaps. Full binary tree: all nodes have 0 or 2 children (not necessarily complete). Perfect binary tree: all levels completely filled. Heap requires complete property for array representation (parent at i, children at 2i+1, 2i+2) to work without gaps.
column14: Perfect tree required for heaps
column15: Complete property: last level must be left-filled without gaps

column2: **Finding maximum path sum in binary tree where path can start and end at any nodes. At each node, decide whether to: (1) include both subtrees (making current node the peak), (2) include one subtree and propagate upward, or (3) start fresh. What's the algorithmic pattern?**
column3: Post-order recursion computing max path sum passing through current node. For each node: max_single_path = max(left_max, right_max, 0) + node.val (can extend upward), max_path_here = left_max + right_max + node.val (current as peak). Update global maximum, return max_single_path upward. Negative sums ignored (start fresh). Time O(n), space O(h).
column14: Preorder traversal with backtracking
column15: Post-order computing single-path vs peak configurations

column2: **AVL tree maintains |height(left) - height(right)| ≤ 1 at every node. Inserting sorted sequence 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 into empty AVL tree. How many rotations occur during insertion?**
column3: Sorted insertion in standard BST creates right-skewed tree. AVL prevents this through rotations. Insert 1: balanced. Insert 2: right-heavy at 1, need left rotation (1 rotation). Insert 3: right-heavy at 1, left rotation (2 total). Pattern continues. For n=7 sorted elements, need approximately n-2 = 5 rotations. Each insertion causes at most one rotation (or double rotation counted as two).
column14: 7 rotations (one per node)

column2: **A UI renders tree nodes in vertical columns. Nodes at same horizontal distance from root form a column. Root at distance 0, left child at -1, right child at +1. For tree with 100K nodes, what determines space complexity of collecting vertical columns?**
column3: Vertical order uses hash map: distance → list of nodes. Space = number of unique distances. Worst case (skewed tree): all nodes at different distances, O(n) space. Best case (complete tree): distances range from -h to +h where h=height, space O(h). For balanced tree with 100K nodes, h≈17, space O(17) for hash keys + O(n) for node lists = O(n) total.
column14: Always O(n) for hash map
column15: O(h) hash keys plus O(n) node storage total O(n)

column2: **BST with 1M nodes must support kth smallest query. Approach 1: In-order traversal until kth element - O(h+k). Approach 2: Augment each node with subtree size, navigate using size info. What's the time complexity improvement?**
column3: Augmented BST: store size of left subtree at each node. To find kth: if k < left_size, recurse left. If k == left_size, current node is answer. If k > left_size, recurse right for (k - left_size - 1)th element. Time O(h), independent of k. For balanced tree, O(log n). In-order approach O(h+k) can be O(n) if k is large. Augmentation enables O(log n) queries.
column14: Augmented BST achieves O(h) independent of k value

column2: **Two binary trees are isomorphic if one can be transformed into other by flipping children at some nodes. Trees: T1: 1→(2→(4,5), 3), T2: 1→(3, 2→(5,4)). To check isomorphism, what must be verified at each node?**
column3: At each node, check: (1) values match, (2) children match in either order (left-left & right-right) OR (left-right & right-left). Recursive check both possibilities. Time O(n). Different from structural equality which requires exact child positions. Isomorphism allows reflection. Example: trees are isomorphic as T2 flips children at root and at node 2.
column14: Check values match and children in either original or swapped order
column15: Requires same height at all nodes

column2: **A DNS lookup system stores 10M domain names in binary tree. Unbalanced tree has O(n) worst-case lookups taking seconds. Balanced tree has O(log n) taking milliseconds. For n=10M, what is the lookup comparison count difference between balanced and worst-case?**
column3: Balanced tree: O(log₂ 10M) ≈ 23 comparisons. Worst case (skewed): O(10M) comparisons. Difference: ~10 million comparisons. This is why production systems use self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black). Single lookup on skewed tree can timeout. Balancing maintains O(log n) guaranteeing performance even with adversarial input.
column14: ~10 million comparison difference (23 vs 10M)

column2: **Given inorder [4,2,5,1,6,3,7] and preorder [1,2,4,5,3,6,7], reconstruct binary tree. Why is preorder first element significant?**
column3: Preorder first element is root. Find root in inorder: elements left of root are left subtree, elements right are right subtree. Recursively construct subtrees. Preorder gives root order, inorder gives left/right division. Both traversals needed - single traversal ambiguous. Time O(n²) naive, O(n) with hash map for inorder positions.

column2: **Cartesian tree from array [3,2,6,1,9] maintains: (1) in-order traversal gives original array, (2) min-heap property (parent < children). What structure results and what's the construction complexity?**
column3: Build using stack: scan array left-to-right, maintain decreasing stack. For element less than stack top, pop until finding smaller element (becomes parent). This creates treap-like structure. Root is minimum element. Construction O(n) using stack. For [3,2,6,1,9]: 1 is root, 2 is left child, 3 is left of 2, 6 is right of 1, 9 is right of 6.

column2: **A 3D game renders only right-most visible nodes at each level (right side view). For tree with 50K nodes, max height 1000, what's the space complexity during level-order traversal to find right-most at each level?**
column3: Level-order BFS uses queue storing one level at time. Maximum queue size = maximum width of tree. For balanced tree (height 1000): width ~2^1000 is astronomical (impossible). For skewed tree: width = 1. Question states max height 1000 suggesting skewed. Queue space O(width). Alternative: preorder with depth tracking uses O(h) recursion space, updating rightmost at each depth. For tall skewed trees, preorder O(h) better than BFS.

column2: **Creating balanced BST from sorted array [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]. Developer creates tree by inserting elements left-to-right. Result is right-skewed O(n) height. What's the correct approach?**
column3: Recursive approach: middle element becomes root (ensures balance), left half recursively becomes left subtree, right half becomes right subtree. For [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]: root=4, left subtree=[1,2,3]→root 2, right subtree=[5,6,7]→root 6. Results in height O(log n). Sequential insertion creates skewed tree. Time O(n), space O(log n) recursion.
column14: Use middle element as root recursively for balance

column2: **Printing tree nodes in zigzag level-order (alternating left-to-right, right-to-left per level). For tree with 1M nodes, what data structure enables this efficiently?**
column3: Deque (double-ended queue) enables efficient zigzag: even levels append right traverse left-to-right, odd levels append left traverse right-to-left. Alternatively: level-order BFS with queue, reverse alternate levels. Both O(n) time. Single queue with level reversal simpler. Deque avoids list reversal overhead. Space O(width) for largest level.
column14: Deque or queue with level reversal achieves O(n)

column2: **Checking if binary tree is mirror symmetric. Tree is symmetric if left subtree mirrors right subtree. What's the recursive relationship?**
column3: Two trees are mirrors if: (1) roots have same value, (2) left subtree of first mirrors right subtree of second, (3) right subtree of first mirrors left subtree of second. Base case: both NULL (symmetric), one NULL other not (asymmetric). Check recursively. Time O(n), space O(h) for recursion. Can also use iterative with queue.
column14: Left subtree mirrors right subtree recursively with cross-comparison

column2: **Removing subtrees that don't contain value 1. Tree: 1→(0→(0,1), 1→(0,1)). After pruning, tree: 1→(0→(None,1), 1→(None,1)). What's the post-order logic?**
column3: Post-order: process children first, then current node. If subtree contains 1, keep it; otherwise return None. Check left, check right, then check current: if current is 1 OR left subtree contains 1 OR right subtree contains 1, keep subtree. Else prune (return None). Must process children first to know if they contain 1.
column14: Post-order: prune leaf-to-root based on whether subtree contains 1

column2: **Company org chart with CEO having 10 direct reports, each having varying reports. Binary tree representation: store first child as left, next sibling as right. For 100K employees, what's the advantage?**
column3: N-ary tree needs variable children list (array/vector) per node - memory overhead for size tracking, dynamic allocation. Binary representation: every node has exactly 2 pointers (first child, next sibling), uniform structure, simpler memory management. Trade-off: traversal less intuitive (right pointer doesn't mean right subtree semantically). Used in compilers for abstract syntax trees.
column14: First-child-next-sibling uses uniform 2-pointer structure vs variable arrays

column2: **Finding diameter of tree AND the actual path forming diameter. Standard approach computes diameter value during height calculation. To also return path, what additional information must be tracked?**
column3: Standard diameter computation updates global maximum (left_height + right_height + 2) but doesn't store path. To reconstruct: track deepest node in left subtree and deepest node in right subtree at each potential diameter node. When updating diameter, store these endpoints. Requires returning (height, deepest_node) from recursion. Space overhead: O(h) for storing endpoints.
column14: Track deepest nodes in both subtrees during height calculation
column15: Requires separate BFS after finding diameter

column3: Complete tree has all levels filled except last, which is left-filled. Binary search on last level using height checks. Compute tree height O(log n). Binary search on last level: check if node exists by following path from root. Total O(log²n). For 1M nodes, ~400 operations vs 1M. Requires checking height of left and right subtrees repeatedly.
